Establishing an end-point scoring protocol for macrocyclic peptide design: size-matched benchmarking, its limits, and a registered prospective test

Carlos Liu¹, Joseph S. Brown¹

¹ Leslie Dan Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada

Draft manuscript — prospective validation section is a registered plan, not yet executed.

Abstract

Macrocyclic peptides engage targets that small molecules cannot, but each analogue is expensive to make, so computational ranking has unusual leverage: a method that merely sorts candidates correctly saves real synthetic effort. Rigorous alchemical free-energy methods achieve this but cost GPU-days per compound. End-point methods such as MM/PBSA cost seconds, and a recent protocol reports strong performance on protein–cyclic-peptide complexes. Whether that performance reflects physics or molecular size has not been established.

Size is not a nuisance variable for peptide binding: larger peptides bury more interface and genuinely bind more tightly. On a five-target benchmark of 234 compounds with measured affinities, experimental ΔG tracks ligand heavy-atom count with a mean within-target Spearman ρ of −0.43, and the MM/PBSA score tracks it more strongly still (ρ = −0.55). Conventional benchmarking therefore cannot separate a scoring function from a ruler.

We resolve this by evaluating only within sets of peptides matched on heavy-atom count, where a size descriptor carries little or no information by construction, and asking how often a method picks the tighter binder of a decisive pair. Within a three-atom window MM/PBSA succeeds in 62.4% of pairs (95% CI 55.5–68.9), against 50% for chance and 83.9% (78.2–88.6) for published FEP+ predictions on the same compounds. At exactly equal heavy-atom count, where a size descriptor is wholly uninformative, the estimate is 60.1% but the interval widens to 47.2–72.0 (posterior mass above chance 0.93) because few same-size decisive pairs exist. Intervals resample compounds rather than pairs, since pairs drawn from a compound set are not independent; resampling pairs understates the width by roughly half.

The skill is modest and unevenly distributed: only PCSK9 (75.7%) is individually above chance, with Cyclin A/B, JAK2, KRAS and MCL-1 each spanning it.

Three further results bear on how such benchmarks should be read. The apparent accuracy depends on the estimator: for KRAS, whose compounds span two receptor crystal forms, pooling gives ρ = +0.225 while averaging within forms gives −0.130, the pooled value being credit for separating two groups offset by 1.15 kcal/mol. The score is a ranking device rather than a free energy, sitting 45–75 kcal/mol from experiment with per-target regression slopes of 0.10–0.21. And on a sixth target held entirely outside development — 17 peptidomimetics against an antibody, affinities sealed before prediction — every method fell below chance and the size–affinity relationship reversed sign, showing that performance on five related targets is not sufficient evidence of transfer.

This method was established to serve an active design campaign: 212 macrocyclic peptides designed against the lipopolysaccharide transport protein LptA, from which candidates will be selected for synthesis and experimental evaluation. We report the protocol applied to that panel, and register the prospective test with its power analysis stated in advance. The purpose of the validation reported here is to establish what the method can and cannot support before committing synthetic resources, not to report a finished prediction.

Keywords: macrocyclic peptides, MM/PBSA, binding affinity, benchmarking, ligand size bias, free energy perturbation

1. Introduction and Background

1.1 Why ranking matters more than prediction here

Macrocyclic and cyclic peptides occupy a chemical space between small molecules and biologics, and they can engage shallow protein–protein interfaces that conventional drugs cannot.(Vinogradov et al., 2019) They are also expensive. A single non-canonical building block can cost on the order of a thousand dollars, synthesis is laborious, and a design campaign can propose hundreds of candidates against a budget of ten. The practical question is therefore not “what is the binding constant?” but “of these candidates, which should we make?”

That is a ranking problem, and ranking is a weaker requirement than prediction. A method that cannot produce a binding constant may still order candidates usefully. Conversely, a method with an impressive correlation coefficient may be useless if that correlation comes from something the chemist already knows.

This work has a specific purpose. We maintain an active design campaign against the lipopolysaccharide transport protein LptA, comprising 212 designed macrocycles from which a subset will be synthesised and assayed. Non-canonical building blocks cost on the order of a thousand dollars each, so the selection is expensive and effectively irreversible. We therefore set out to establish, in advance of that commitment, exactly what an end-point scoring protocol can and cannot support on this chemistry — which is a methods question, and is the subject of this paper. The design campaign is described in Section 4 and the registered prospective test in Section 5; the validation that precedes them is what licenses either.

1.2 The computational options

Free energy perturbation (FEP) is the rigorous approach: it simulates one ligand transforming into another and tracks the free-energy change. Applied to macrocycles with appropriate enhanced sampling, FEP+ achieves a global pairwise RMSE of 1.06 kcal/mol across more than 230 analogues spanning over 10 kcal/mol of experimental range.(Awoonor-Williams et al., 2026) The cost is GPU-days per compound and a commercial licence.

End-point methods take the opposite trade. MM/PBSA evaluates the interaction energy of a single structure and subtracts an estimate of the desolvation cost, in seconds rather than days.(Genheden & Ryde, 2015) Zhao and colleagues recently reported a fine-tuned MM/PBSA(GBSA) workflow for protein–cyclic-peptide complexes achieving a Pearson correlation of −0.732 against experimental affinity on a 50-complex dataset, roughly twice that of a conventional docking score, at about three seconds per prediction.(Zhao et al., 2025)

The gap between these is roughly three orders of magnitude in cost. What is given up is not well characterised for peptides.

1.3 The problem with the obvious benchmark

Scoring functions have a long-documented tendency to track molecular size. Jacobsson and Karlén found “a high to intermediate linear correlation between the score and the number of heavy atoms” for nine of ten scoring functions tested, and identified this ligand bias as a source of false positives in virtual screening.(Jacobsson & Karlén, 2006) The standard responses are normalisation by molecular weight or heavy-atom count, ligand efficiency metrics, or matched-pair benchmark design.(Jacobsson & Karlén, 2006; Kalinowsky et al., 2018)

For peptides the problem is sharper, for a reason that is easy to miss. Size is not an artefact here. More residues bury more interface area, and buried area is a genuine driver of binding affinity. A size descriptor is therefore a mediator of the physics, not a confounder to be regressed away — and partialling it out over-corrects, removing exactly the signal a physics method is supposed to capture.

This creates a genuine methodological difficulty. Comparing a scoring function against a heavy-atom count across compounds of different sizes is unfair in both directions: the scoring function gets credit for re-reading size, and the control gets credit for real physics.

1.4 What we do

We hold size fixed. Within each target we compare only peptides of identical heavy-atom count, where a size descriptor has no information at all because there is no size difference to read, and ask the question a chemist actually asks: given two candidates, which binds tighter? This extends matched-pair benchmarking(Kalinowsky et al., 2018) to macrocyclic peptides, where the size range is far wider than in small-molecule series and the synthesis stakes are higher.

We report: a replication of the Zhao protocol on an independent five-target cohort; the magnitude of the size confound; size-matched performance against a published FEP+ ceiling on identical compounds; the sensitivity of all of this to the choice of statistical estimator; and an application to a de novo design campaign against LptA, with a registered prospective test.

Box 1 — What a force field is, for readers new to this

A force field is a set of rules for computing the energy of an arrangement of atoms. It assigns each atom a partial electric charge and a size, and each bond a stiffness and a preferred length. Given the 3-D coordinates of a protein and a peptide, it returns a number: how favourable that arrangement is. It is classical physics — balls and springs — with parameters fitted to quantum calculations and experiment. It knows nothing about biology.

Standard amino acids have well-tested parameters. Non-canonical residues do not, and must be parameterised individually before anything can be computed (Section 2.3).

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Benchmark cohort

Method development and all reported statistics use a published external benchmark: the five-target macrocycle and cyclic-peptide series of Awoonor-Williams and colleagues — KRAS, PCSK9, MCL-1, JAK2 and Cyclin A/B — comprising over 230 peptidic and non-peptidic analogues.(Awoonor-Williams et al., 2026) We use the 241 compounds for which structures and labels could be assembled; the attrition to the analysed sets is given below.

Two properties make this the right cohort. The affinities were measured by a third party, so the evaluation cannot be tuned to them. And because FEP+ predictions were published alongside, a rigorous-method ceiling is available on exactly the same compounds, which is otherwise difficult to obtain.

Compound attrition, stated once for reproducibility. Of the 241 compounds for which structures and labels could be assembled, 235 carry an experimental binding free energy; 234 remain after excluding MCL_1__cpd_55 for an unrelieved steric clash (Section 2.2); and 220 remain for the pairwise analyses, which additionally exclude censored measurements because the ordering of a censored pair is ambiguous. Correlation analyses in §3.1–3.3 use the 234; pairwise analyses in §3.4 use the 220. Every reported n refers to one of these two sets.

Compounds are not independent within a target: two targets span more than one receptor crystal form (KRAS, two; PCSK9, three), giving eight receptor groups. All primary statistics are computed within receptor group and averaged with equal weight per target (Section 2.6).

2.2 Structure preparation

Receptor and peptide are cleaned with pdb4amber in two passes. The first retains prepared hydrogens so that histidine tautomer and cystine assignments carry into residue names; the second strips hydrogens so that tleap rebuilds them against its own templates. A single pass is insufficient because prepared files carry atoms (e.g. HXT) for which the older force fields have no type.

Cyclisation is imposed explicitly. Head-to-tail macrocycles receive an explicit bond in tleap; disulfide-cyclised peptides are detected geometrically (S–S < 2.5 Å) and left to the CONECT records written by pdb4amber, because re-issuing those bonds manually produces 1-4: cannot add bond errors. For macrocycles with uncharged termini, clearPdbResMap prevents tleap applying terminal templates to a molecule that has no termini.

Two preparation defects were found during validation, both of which produced plausible but wrong energies, and both of which are corrected here:

Spurious chain breaks. pdb4amber inserted TER records into continuous chains, each of which tleap capped, producing complexes with initial energies above 10¹⁷ kcal/mol. The problem affects 14 of 50 reference complexes, with 9 to 25 spurious records each (the remaining 36 are unaffected). TER records whose flanking C–N distance is below 2.0 Å are deleted. After the fix, atom counts of a reference complex match published values exactly.

Unrelieved steric clash. One compound (MCL_1__cpd_55) passed the pipeline’s own ok status while carrying a van der Waals term of +277,293 kcal/mol, against ≤ −50 kcal/mol for every other compound. A status check does not test for unrelieved overlap. Screening on VDWAALS > 0 is mandatory before any analysis and is applied throughout. Rank statistics are largely insensitive to this compound (macro Spearman 0.532 → 0.545), but the pooled Pearson correlation moves from −0.048 to +0.265 on removing it, and MCL-1’s Pearson r from −0.124 to +0.693. A single unrelieved clash was therefore enough to make the method look uncorrelated with experiment.

2.3.1 Non-canonical residue parameterisation

Designed peptides carrying non-standard residues cannot be scored until each residue has Amber parameters. The LptA application required 170 non-standard residues (165 unique non-canonical codes plus five residues constituting the thanatin derivative-7 scaffold, none of which tleap knows). Because this step gates everything downstream and is where most silent failures occur, we specify it in full.

Protocol, per residue.

  1. Take the polymer-form rotamer and the corresponding chemistry definition from the source library. Atom names and bond orders are read from the definition file, not perceived from coordinates; coordinates are matched positionally.
  2. Cap with ACE at the N-terminus and NME at the C-terminus, giving a neutral dipeptide. Cap atoms are placed by bisector construction with a hard clash check, and cap atom names are chosen per residue to avoid collisions with side-chain names.
  3. Derive AM1-BCC charges on the capped dipeptide with antechamber, under element-safe placeholder atom names (see defect 1 below).
  4. Restore the true atom names, case-insensitively.
  5. Reassign the backbone to protein atom types (N, H, CA, HA, C, O) while the side chain remains GAFF2. Cap atoms are retyped as protein types as well, because they stand in for neighbouring residues and leaving them GAFF2-typed makes parmchk2 generate cross terms against the wrong types.
  6. Run prepgen with a mainchain file (HEAD_NAME N, TAIL_NAME C, OMIT_NAME for the caps, CHARGE 0.0) to remove the caps and redistribute their charge, giving a residue that nets zero.
  7. Run parmchk2 for missing GAFF2 terms, then strip from the resulting frcmod any entry that would redefine a protein backbone type.

Capping matters because AM1-BCC on a free amino acid fits backbone charges in an environment (–NH₂ / –COOH) the residue never occupies; capping places the charge fit in a peptide-like context, which is the standard Amber construction for non-standard residues.(Cieplak et al., 1995) Backbone retyping matters because antechamber otherwise types the backbone as GAFF2 and tleap then has no parameters across the peptide bond to a neighbouring standard residue (Could not find bond parameter for atom types: C - ns). The alpha carbon is typed CT under ff03/ff99 and CX under ff14SB/ff19SB — ff03 has no CX at all — so two complete parameter sets are maintained and a prep typed for one force field fails on the other.

Validation gate. Each residue is tested by constructing ALA–X–ALA in tleap and requiring zero missing parameters. All 170 pass under both backbone typings. This gate is not optional: tleap writes a topology even when parameters are missing, substituting defaults silently, so “the build succeeded” is not evidence of correctness.

Failure modes. Six defects were found, four of which produced plausible output rather than an error. We tabulate them because every one is a property of the standard toolchain rather than of our library, and will recur for anyone attempting this.

**Table 1: Silent and overt failure modes in non-canonical residue parameterisation.

# defect how it manifests detection remedy
1 antechamber infers element from atom name every alpha carbon (CA) read as calcium; 61 aromatic carbons named CL* read as chlorine; FE, NI, CO likewise element census against the chemistry definition build under element-safe placeholder names, restore afterwards
2 bond orders perceived from geometry fails on hypervalent sulfur (sulfonamides) and iodoaryls valence check supply bond orders from the definition via MOL2
3 fixed-dihedral cap placement NME nitrogen placed 0.15 Å from the residue’s own carbonyl oxygen whenever ψ ≈ 180° inter-atomic distance check after capping bisector placement with a clash threshold
4 cap atom names collide with side-chain names 75 of 170 residues affected name-set intersection per-residue cap naming
5 library-internal name inconsistency nine halogenated residues: the rotamer PDB truncates CLM1 to CLM, and one residue names both chlorines CLM. Unmatched atoms are dropped silently by prepgen, surfacing later as a nan internal coordinate cross-check names between definition and coordinates take names and bonds from the definition, match coordinates positionally

A limitation we could not remove. GAFF2 has no selenium and sqm has no AM1 parameters for it, so antechamber retypes selenium as sulfur and parmchk2 reports nothing missing — the build appears clean. Two residues are affected and are flagged ok_element_unsupported rather than shipped as validated. Any score involving them is an approximation, and we say so wherever such a residue appears.

2.4 Energy minimisation

Minimisation follows the published settings — imin=1, maxcyc=5000, ncyc=2000, cut=1000.0, igb=2 — corresponding to 2000 steps of steepest descent then conjugate gradient in the Onufriev–Bashford–Case generalised Born model(Onufriev et al., 2004) with no nonbonded cutoff.

Because the available AmberTools build does not ship pmemd.cuda, and sander requires hours per complex at cut=1000, minimisation is performed in OpenMM(Eastman et al., 2017) using OBC1 and NoCutoff, the direct equivalents. The two engines are not identical, so the OpenMM L-BFGS iteration count was calibrated against sander by structural drift: sander’s 5000 cycles move the complex 0.84 Å RMSD, an unrestricted OpenMM minimisation 1.25 Å. A cap of 500 iterations reproduces sander’s drift and is used throughout.

This calibration is load-bearing. On KRAS, removing the cap changes the correlation from +0.225 to +0.529, and the spread introduced by the stopping point (SD 3.60 kcal/mol) is as large as the entire between-compound signal (SD 3.53) — a ratio of 1.02. Removing the cap does not generalise: it improves KRAS by +0.304 and degrades PCSK9 by −0.280, for a net macro change of −0.009 (cluster bootstrap +0.110, 95% CI [−0.066, +0.230]).

2.5 Free-energy evaluation

MMPBSA.py(Miller et al., 2012) is run single-trajectory, so receptor internal energy cancels exactly. Poisson–Boltzmann calculations use the internal solver with interior dielectric 2.0, exterior 80.0, and the LCPO nonpolar model (inp=1, cavity_surften=0.0072, cavity_offset=0). Arms at εᵢₙ = 1 and 4 and GB arms are computed in parallel for comparison. No entropy term is included, following the source protocol.

The intdiel keyword is silently ignored by both engines when passed through &pb. The dielectric is therefore set by writing use_sander=1, generating inputs with -make-mdins, injecting intdiel into the generated _MM_gb.mdin, and re-running with -use-mdins. Without this, every “different dielectric” arm silently returns identical numbers.

The protocol is single-structure: one minimised geometry is scored, not an ensemble. MMPBSA.py reports Calculations performed using 1.0 complex frames with zero standard error. This is the source protocol’s design, stated explicitly because “MM/PBSA” usually implies ensemble averaging. The choice is defensible on published evidence that MM/PBSA correlation does not generally improve with longer sampling because the limiting error is bias rather than variance;(Genheden & Ryde, 2015) we tested it directly (Section 3.7).

Box 2 — What MM/PBSA actually computes

Take the structure of the peptide sitting in the protein’s binding site. Add up the electrostatic and van der Waals attraction between them: that is the gas-phase interaction energy, and it is always favourable. But in water, both surfaces are coated with ordered water molecules that must be stripped off before they can touch, and that costs energy. MM/PBSA estimates this desolvation penalty by solving the Poisson–Boltzmann equation, treating water as a continuous dielectric rather than individual molecules.

The binding score is attraction minus desolvation. What it omits is entropy — the freedom the peptide loses when it stops tumbling in solution and locks into one conformation. That omission is why the numbers are not free energies (Section 3.4).

2.5.1 Machine-learned force-field scoring

To test whether the end-point method’s limits are a property of the energy function rather than of end-point scoring itself, the same minimised geometries were rescored with SO3LR-SF,(Agha et al., 2026) a scoring function built on a machine-learned force field trained on quantum-chemical reference data with explicit long-range electrostatics and dispersion. It is the strongest available test of that question: it replaces the molecular-mechanics energy function entirely while keeping the single-structure, end-point framing.

Each complex was split into receptor and ligand from the minimised coordinates — the identical input MM/PBSA scores, so the comparison isolates the energy function — with formal charges taken from the Amber topologies and passed explicitly (--charge-lig, --charge-prot, --charge-cpx). The published command-line interface was used at its validated 8 Å trimming radius (--trim 8). All 241 cohort complexes scored successfully at a mean of 19.6 s each on 24 CPU cores; JAX fell back to CPU execution, consistent with the 1–10 s per complex the authors report for CPU.

Implementation note. The released CLI raises 'Namespace' object has no attribute 'radius' after computing the energy, leaving results_summary.json zero-length. The binding energy is therefore parsed from the Binding energy: X kcal/mol line the tool emits immediately before the failure. This is a reporting bug downstream of the calculation, not an error in it, but it means the documented output path cannot be used as-is.

Because SO3LR-SF is evaluated on exactly the cohort, compound sets and estimators defined above, it is reported as a direct substitution and not as a separate benchmark.

2.6 Statistical evaluation

Primary estimator. Spearman’s ρ computed within receptor group and averaged across targets, each target weighted equally. Pooling compounds across targets is rejected: it rewards a method for knowing that one series is systematically more potent than another, which is not the question a design campaign asks. Section 3.2 quantifies the resulting inflation within our own data.

Size-matched pairwise accuracy — the primary measure. For each target we enumerate all compound pairs whose measured affinities differ by at least a margin m (“decisive” pairs) and whose ligand heavy-atom counts differ by at most a window w. For each pair we ask whether the method orders them correctly. Chance is 0.5. At w = 0 a size descriptor is undefined, because there is no size difference to read.

Two free parameters enter here, and neither was chosen after seeing the result.

The affinity margin m. Pairs whose measured affinities are nearly equal cannot discriminate between methods and only add noise, so a margin is required. We set m = 0.5 kcal/mol a priori because it is approximately the reproducibility of the assays contributing to the cohort, and report the full sensitivity in Table 2 rather than a single value. The conclusion is stable: MM/PBSA is above chance at every margin from 0 to 1.5 kcal/mol.

The size window w. We report w = 0, the strictest possible matching, and w = 3, which admits enough pairs for the macro interval to be informative. Both are reported throughout; we do not select between them on the basis of which is more favourable.

margin (kcal/mol) pairs MM/PBSA 95% CI heavy atoms edge FEP+
0.00 2384 0.597 [0.542, 0.649] 0.585 +0.012 0.769
0.25 2002 0.613 [0.554, 0.674] 0.591 +0.022 0.805
0.50 1645 0.624 [0.553, 0.691] 0.602 +0.022 0.839

Two features of Table 2 deserve comment, and one of them is unfavourable. Accuracy rises monotonically with the margin up to 1.5 kcal/mol for both MM/PBSA and FEP+, which is the behaviour of a real but noisy signal: pairs that are further apart in affinity are easier to order. But at the chosen margin the edge over a heavy-atom count is only +0.022. It becomes substantial (+0.07 to +0.20) only for pairs separated by 1 kcal/mol or more. The method’s advantage over the trivial descriptor within a three-atom window is therefore real but small, and concentrated in the pairs that are easiest to tell apart. At w = 0, where the descriptor has no information at all, the comparison does not arise.

Uncertainty. All pairwise intervals resample compounds, not pairs. This matters: the n(n−1)/2 pairs formed from n compounds are not independent draws, because every compound appears in many pairs. Resampling pairs treats them as independent and badly understates the uncertainty — on the exact-match band it returns [0.530, 0.693] where the correct compound-level interval is [0.472, 0.720]. We resample compounds within each target (2,000 draws), rebuild the pair set from each resample, and combine targets for macro values (5,000 draws). Where Spearman correlations are reported the bootstrap resamples receptor groups.

Controls. Ligand heavy-atom count is computed on the same compounds with the same estimator throughout. Censored measurements are retained and flagged in correlation analyses and excluded from pairwise analyses where the ordering would be ambiguous.

Box 3 — How to read a pairwise accuracy

Hand the method two peptides whose measured affinities genuinely differ, and ask which binds tighter. Do that for every such pair. The fraction it gets right is the pairwise accuracy.

A coin gets 50%. A perfect method gets 100%. 60% means that in a head-to-head choice between two candidates, the method is right three times in five instead of one in two. That is a modest edge, but across a campaign of many such choices it is not nothing — and crucially it is measured here in a setting where the obvious shortcut, “pick the bigger one”, is unavailable.

3. Results and Discussion

3.1 The protocol reproduces, with a caveat on what is being reproduced

Scoring the source protocol’s 50-complex Dataset I under ff03 with PB at εᵢₙ = 2 gives a Pearson correlation of −0.382, against the −0.545 reported for the equivalent arm.(Zhao et al., 2025) The headline −0.732 in that work is a two-step workflow that first re-ranks docked poses and then scores the selected pose; our evaluation scores the deposited pose directly, so the two numbers are not comparable and we do not treat the gap as a replication failure.

Transferring the protocol unchanged to the independent five-target cohort gives a macro Spearman ρ of +0.545 across 234 compounds (Figure 3; per-target values in Table 3).

**Table 3: Per-target performance on the Awoonor-Williams cohort. Pearson r and Spearman ρ are computed within receptor group. “Slope” is the per-target regression slope of score on experiment; its reciprocal gives the factor by which ΔΔG spread is inflated.

target n MM/PBSA r R² MM/PBSA ρ FEP+ ρ slope offset (kcal/mol)
Cyclin A/B 21 +0.609 0.371 +0.591 +0.791 0.202 −59.4
JAK2 48 +0.588 0.345 +0.595 +0.788 0.103 −44.8
KRAS 45 +0.300 0.090 +0.225 +0.786 0.125 −74.8
MCL-1 57 +0.693 0.480 +0.728 +0.859 0.099 −69.0
PCSK9 63 +0.551 0.304 +0.584 +0.929 0.208 −64.9
macro 234 +0.548 0.318 +0.545 +0.831 — —

Two things in Table 3 deserve emphasis. First, the commonly quoted “R” in such analyses is a correlation, not a coefficient of determination: r = 0.548 corresponds to R² = 0.318, so the protocol explains under a third of the variance, against 0.719 for FEP+. Second, the per-target slopes of 0.10–0.21 mean the score’s ΔΔG spread is inflated five- to tenfold, and the offsets of 45–75 kcal/mol are the signature of the omitted entropy term.

3.2 How you average changes the answer

Pooling compounds that come from different receptor structures inflates the apparent correlation, and KRAS shows this cleanly because its 45 compounds are split across two crystal forms.

**Table 4: KRAS under two estimators. Pooling reverses the sign of the result.

KRAS n MM/PBSA ρ FEP+ ρ
within form 7YUZ 17 −0.307 +0.576
within form 8JJS 28 +0.046 +0.782
macro over forms 45 −0.130 +0.679
pooled over both 45 +0.225 +0.786

The mechanism is explicit: the MM/PBSA score is offset by −3.05 kcal/mol between the two forms, in the same direction as a −1.15 kcal/mol offset in the experimental labels. The pooled +0.225 is therefore credit for separating two groups, not for ranking within either. FEP+ is far less affected (+0.679 versus +0.786), as expected of a method whose signal does not come from a group offset.

This matters beyond KRAS because it occurs inside what is conventionally reported as a within-family metric. Any benchmark of this kind must state which estimator it uses; we use within-receptor averaging throughout.

3.3 Size is a real driver of binding, and the score tracks it

Figure 2 quantifies the confound. Experimental ΔG tracks ligand heavy-atom count with a mean within-target Spearman ρ of −0.43 (panel A; negative because more atoms give more negative ΔG). The MM/PBSA score tracks heavy-atom count more strongly still, at −0.55 (panel B).

The first of these is physics, not bias: more residues bury more interface area. The second means the score and the trivial descriptor are substantially measuring the same thing. Under the conventional estimator, a heavy-atom count reaches ρ = 0.488 pooled in-family and 0.613 within receptor — numerically better than MM/PBSA’s 0.459 within receptor.

That comparison is not evidence that the physics is useless. It is evidence that the comparison is ill-posed. Both quantities partly measure size; the one that measures it more directly wins on a benchmark where size varies. Panel C shows that enough compounds share a heavy-atom count within each target to make a fair comparison possible.

3.4 Size-matched performance: the primary result

**Table 5: Pairwise accuracy on decisive pairs (|ΔΔG| ≥ 0.5 kcal/mol). Chance = 0.500. Intervals are 95% bootstrap over compounds (Section 2.6). The left block is the strictest matching; the right admits a three-atom window and is better powered.

target MM/PBSA, identical size 95% CI MM/PBSA, within 3 atoms 95% CI
Cyclin A/B 0.533 [0.053, 1.000] 0.674 [0.454, 0.863]
JAK2 0.637 [0.397, 0.831] 0.598 [0.437, 0.732]
KRAS 0.518 [0.289, 0.727] 0.496 [0.339, 0.664]
MCL-1 0.549 [0.328, 0.757] 0.594 [0.444, 0.733]
PCSK9 0.765 [0.613, 0.882] 0.757 [0.671, 0.830]
macro, MM/PBSA 0.601 [0.472, 0.720] 0.624 [0.555, 0.689]
macro, FEP+ 0.841 [0.730, 0.912] 0.839 [0.782, 0.886]

The two bands give different levels of confidence, and we report both rather than the more favourable one. At exact size matching the macro estimate is 0.601 but its interval includes chance; the posterior mass above 0.5 is 0.93. There are only 337 decisive pairs in that band, drawn from few enough compounds that the compound-level interval is wide. At a three-atom window — still tight relative to a 25-to-127 heavy-atom cohort, and still a regime in which a size descriptor achieves only 0.602 — the macro estimate is 0.624 with an interval that excludes chance and posterior mass above 0.5 exceeding 0.999.

The honest summary is therefore: the skill is established at near-matched size and suggestive but not conclusive at exactly matched size**, the latter limited by how few same-size decisive pairs the cohort contains rather than by the size of the effect.

The skill is also unevenly distributed, and under compound-level resampling only PCSK9 is individually above chance — at both bands. JAK2’s point estimate of 0.637 at exact matching has an interval of [0.397, 0.831] and cannot be separated from chance on its own; the same is true of Cyclin A/B, KRAS and MCL-1. The macro result at the three-atom band is therefore driven by PCSK9 with weak support from the others, not by uniform performance.

One candidate explanation is interface polarity, since a continuum-solvent treatment should add most where desolvation dominates. PCSK9 does have much the most polar interface in the cohort (median buried-area polarity 42.2%, against 30.5% for the next-highest). But the explanation does not survive the other cases: JAK2 is the fourth most polar of the five (23.8%) yet has the second-highest point estimate at exact matching, while KRAS is the second most polar (30.5%) and sits at chance in both bands. This was tested with two definitions of polarity, not one. The figures above use the polar fraction of the interface that is buried on binding. We also computed the descriptor reported to predict per-target performance for machine-learned scoring — polar SASA divided by total SASA of the binding pocket(Agha et al., 2026) — from scratch for all 241 complexes. It gives the same answer: r = −0.483 (p = 0.41) against macro ρ and +0.363 (p = 0.55) against pairwise accuracy, against −0.353 and +0.520 for the interface descriptor. The two descriptors correlate at r = +0.77 across the five targets, so they order the targets similarly and the conclusion never depended on which was used. Polarity alone therefore does not account for where the method works, and with five targets we cannot identify what does. We report the pattern without an explanation rather than offer one the data does not support.

The behaviour of the control across matching bands is itself informative. As the permitted size difference widens from zero to three to five heavy atoms to unrestricted, the heavy-atom count climbs from undefined, to 0.602, to 0.629, to 0.717, while MM/PBSA moves only from 0.601 to 0.738. The control gains almost all of its apparent performance from size variation; the scoring function does not.

3.5 What the score is not

With entropy omitted, the raw score is not a free energy. It sits 45–75 kcal/mol from experimental ΔG (Table 3), and matching the experimental scale requires fitting a slope and intercept within a target, which requires compounds already measured in that series. An RMSE of 1.11 kcal/mol is achievable only after that fit. It is not a prospective accuracy, and should not be quoted as one.

3.6 Force-field choice does not transfer

On the benchmark, ff03 outperforms ff19SB (0.545 versus 0.495 macro, winning four of five targets; only JAK2 prefers ff19SB, +0.604 versus +0.595). On the LptA design panel the ordering reverses, with ff19SB ≥ ff14SB > ff03 in every branch.

This inversion should not be over-read. The LptA designs have no measured affinities, so that comparison is scored against Rosetta dG_separated. We tested that reference directly on 239 benchmark compounds where measured affinities exist and found a macro Spearman of −0.149, wrong-signed on four of five targets, and below a heavy-atom count (+0.487). A reference standard that does not itself track experiment cannot establish which force field is better.

We report the comparison only as a caution: force-field selections made on one dataset should not be assumed to transfer, and we do not claim ff19SB is superior for these designs.

3.6.1 A machine-learned force field does not rescue the ranking

If the ceiling in Section 3.4 came from the molecular-mechanics energy function, a machine-learned force field should raise it. It does not.

SO3LR-SF is reported at Spearman 0.51 against MM/GBSA 0.44 and Glide 0.27 on its own eight-target benchmark of drug-like small molecules.(Agha et al., 2026) On our five macrocycle targets it reaches a macro Spearman of 0.292 — below every molecular-mechanics variant we computed (0.427 to 0.545) and below a heavy-atom count (0.487). The comparator reproduces: our MM/GBSA arm gives 0.478 against the 0.44 they report, so the shortfall is specific to the new method rather than an artefact of an inflated baseline.

method macro ρ accuracy, |Δheavy| = 0 accuracy, |Δheavy| ≤ 3
FEP+ (published) 0.831 0.841 [0.730, 0.912] 0.839 [0.782, 0.886]
MM/PBSA (this work) 0.545 0.601 [0.472, 0.720] 0.624 [0.555, 0.689]
heavy-atom count 0.487 undefined 0.602 [0.524, 0.677]
MM/GBSA (this work) 0.478 — —
SO3LR-SF 0.292 0.597 [0.484, 0.709] 0.576 [0.503, 0.648]

MM/PBSA and FEP+ rows reproduce Table 5 exactly; the SO3LR-SF row was computed by the same script, estimator and bootstrap seed, so the three are directly comparable.

On size-matched pairs SO3LR-SF is indistinguishable from MM/PBSA at exact matching (0.597 versus 0.601) and lower in the three-atom band (0.576 versus 0.624), where it also falls below the trivial size descriptor. It is no less size-driven: its correlation with heavy-atom count is −0.589, against MM/PBSA’s −0.577. Replacing the energy function does not address the confound this paper is about.

At target level the two methods look complementary, and they are not. SO3LR-SF is the best non-FEP method on MCL-1 (ρ = 0.772 against MM/PBSA’s 0.728), but inverts on KRAS (−0.106) and falls to zero on PCSK9 (−0.035) — precisely the target where MM/PBSA is strongest (pairwise accuracy 0.757). That pattern suggests the two fail on different cases and could be combined.

We tested it directly rather than leaving the suggestion standing, and it does not hold. Within each receptor the two methods’ rank errors correlate at +0.714: they are largely wrong about the same compounds, and the apparent complementarity is an artefact of comparing per-target aggregates rather than compound-level errors. An equal-weight consensus of within-receptor rank z-scores is accordingly worse than MM/PBSA alone — macro ρ 0.445 against 0.545, and pairwise accuracy 0.610 against 0.624 in the three-atom band — with no gain at exact matching (0.597 against 0.601). A MM/PBSA + MM/GBSA consensus, included as a control, behaves the same way (0.513, 0.622) at a rank-error correlation of +0.920.

The practical consequence is that there is no cheap ensemble route to the FEP+ ceiling here. Averaging end-point scores does not help when their errors are shared, and on this cohort they are shared whether the underlying energy function is molecular-mechanical or machine-learned.

We report this as a negative result on a published method applied outside its validated domain, not as a criticism of it. Its benchmark is drug-like small molecules; macrocyclic peptides with non-canonical residues and net charge are out of that distribution, which is exactly why the test is informative for the present purpose.

3.7 Longer sampling does not help

A natural objection to single-structure scoring is that an ensemble average would do better. We tested this on 40 KRAS compounds for which four independent 10 ns explicit-solvent replicas were available, scored over the 2–10 ns window at 81 frames per replica — 324 frames per compound.

The ensemble does not converge well enough for the averaging to help. The median replicate-to-replicate standard deviation of the ensemble score is 6.81 kcal/mol, while the standard deviation between compounds is 5.74 kcal/mol. The noise from which replicas you happened to run is therefore larger than the entire signal distinguishing one compound from another, a ratio of 1.19. Splitting by panel, the 20 confirmatory compounds give 5.60 against 5.54 (ratio 1.01) and the 20 primary compounds 8.70 against 4.88 (ratio 1.78); the conclusion does not depend on the subset.

Four 10 ns replicas is a substantial sampling budget for a system of this size, and it is not enough to make the ensemble score reproducible at the resolution the ranking requires. This is consistent with the general finding that MM/PBSA correlation does not improve reliably with longer sampling because the limiting error is bias rather than variance,(Genheden & Ryde, 2015) and it supports the source protocol’s single-structure design on pragmatic grounds: a cheaper calculation that is reproducible is preferable to an expensive one that is not.

3.8 An external test on a sixth target

The five benchmark targets are congeneric medicinal-chemistry series against folded pockets, assembled by one group for one FEP+ campaign. They may resemble each other more than they resemble a new target. We therefore tested the pipeline on a sixth system held entirely outside development: 17 peptidomimetics against the anti-haemagglutinin antibody 12CA5, with binding measured by biolayer interferometry (7 binders spanning 0.21–77 nM, 10 non-binders). Affinities were sealed before any prediction was made.

Every method failed, and several inverted.

**Table 6: Performance on the sealed 12CA5 panel. Directions were fixed before unblinding.

method ρ vs pK_D (7 binders) binder/non-binder AUC
heavy-atom count −0.750 0.257
molecular weight −0.750 0.271
chemical model (pAffinity) −0.107 0.214
chemical model (rank score) −0.306 0.200

Chance AUC is 0.5; every value is below it. The tightest binder (0.21 nM) was ranked 16th of 17 by every method, and top-5 overlap with the experimental top 5 was zero throughout.

Two findings matter for the present work. First, the size–affinity relationship reversed sign: heavy-atom count correlates at −0.750 here against +0.49 to +0.61 on the benchmark. Size is predictive in congeneric series elaborated into a pocket, and anti-predictive against a compact epitope groove where bulk is in the way. A method whose signal is partly size therefore carries a sign that is target-dependent and not knowable in advance without measurement — which is a further argument for evaluating at fixed size.

Second, MM/PBSA could not be scored reliably at all: 3 of 17 built poses carried positive van der Waals terms and were excluded by the screen of Section 2.2, one failed to score, and across the remainder the score correlated with the pose builder’s clash count at ρ = −0.891. Those peptidomimetics were threaded onto a template they do not match. The lesson is that end-point scoring inherits the quality of its input pose, and that pose provenance must be reported alongside any score (Section 4).

We present this as a limitation rather than a general claim: one external target with 17 compounds cannot establish how the method behaves on all new systems. It does establish that benchmark performance on five related targets is not sufficient evidence of transfer.

3.9 The campaign this method serves: de novo macrocycles against LptA

Lipopolysaccharide transport protein A (LptA) is the periplasmic component of the seven-protein Lpt bridge that moves lipopolysaccharide from the inner membrane to the cell surface in Gram-negative bacteria. The insect-derived antimicrobial peptide thanatin binds the N-terminal β-strand of LptA, disrupting both LptA–LptA dimerisation and the LptC–LptA interaction and causing LptA degradation.(Moura et al., 2020) Because that β-strand edge is also the dimerisation interface, the site is a template for designed β-hairpin binders, and thanatin analogues optimised against carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae have been characterised structurally and thermodynamically.(Oi et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2021)

The protocol above was established in order to triage this panel. We applied it to 212 designed macrocycles in three branches: 20 canonical head-to-tail cyclic peptides from generative backbone design followed by sequence design; 96 single-residue non-canonical substitutions on those canonical parents; and 96 single-residue non-canonical substitutions on a thanatin derivative-7 scaffold templated on a co-crystal structure. A total of 213 complexes were scored — the 212 designs plus the derivative-7 parent as a reference.

Pose quality. Unlike the benchmark, these poses are generated rather than crystallographic, which raises the question of whether scores read binding or pose-construction artefact. Across all 213 scored complexes the built poses contain zero interface heavy-atom contacts below 1.8 Å, and minimisation drift spans only 0.49–1.42 Å. For comparison, the 12CA5 panel of Section 3.8, whose peptidomimetics were threaded onto a non-matching template, showed 0–44 clashes per complex, backbone RMSD to 4.72 Å, and MM/PBSA scores correlating with clash count at ρ = −0.891 — that is, reading pose quality rather than chemistry. The LptA poses show no such pathology, which is a necessary condition for the scores to be interpretable, though not a sufficient one.

Size dependence differs by branch. The score’s correlation with ligand heavy-atom count is −0.668 for the 20 canonical de novo designs, −0.606 for their 96 non-canonical swaps, and only −0.291 for the 96 thanatin swaps. This follows from construction: single substitutions on a fixed 16-residue scaffold barely change size, whereas the de novo designs vary from 14 to 18 residues. The thanatin branch is therefore the least size-confounded, and by the argument of Section 3.4 it is the branch on which the protocol’s demonstrated skill is most likely to apply.

No measured affinities exist for any of these designs. All statements about them are computational, and the protocol has not demonstrated predictive skill on this system. Rankings are reported within branch only; the branches occupy different score ranges and pooling them produces a spurious correlation.

3.10 Committed prospective test (registered; synthesis pending)

This section describes a committed experiment that has not yet been executed. No results exist at the time of writing, and none are claimed.

Everything above is retrospective, on compounds measured by others. The campaign of Section 4 will proceed to synthesis, and we register the forward test here, before any compound is made, so that the prediction cannot be adjusted after the fact.

Design. Ten de novo LptA designs, selected and frozen before synthesis, will be made and assayed. The ranking is registered at the point of selection and will not be revised.

Compound selection. The ten span a four-heavy-atom window (149–153 atoms) — essentially size-matched, which is the regime in which Section 3.4 establishes skill — while covering 34 kcal/mol of predicted score range (−104.0 to −69.8 kcal/mol). Spanning the predicted range rather than selecting predicted winners is deliberate: a set of predicted winners cannot falsify the ranking.

What ten compounds can and cannot establish. Power analysis by simulation, at the effect size measured here (ρ ≈ 0.30, corresponding to ~60% pairwise accuracy):

**Table 7: Simulated power to detect a positive rank correlation at p < 0.05.

n power at ρ = 0.30 ρ = 0.50 ρ = 0.75
10 0.12 0.28 0.67
20 0.22 0.58 0.96
40 0.43 0.88 1.00

Ten compounds cannot confirm the ranking: at the measured effect size the power is 12%, so a null result would be uninformative. We state this in advance rather than discovering it afterwards. Ten compounds can, however, do two useful things: detect a catastrophic inversion (66% power against ρ = −0.75), which is a live concern because exactly such a reversal occurred on the external target of Section 3.8; and supply ten measured anchors that permit within-series calibration.

This test is therefore registered as a sanity check and anchor acquisition, not as confirmatory validation. Confirmatory validation would require approximately 40 compounds, and we do not claim it here.

3.11 Synthesis of findings

The central finding is that end-point MM/PBSA retains genuine ranking skill on macrocyclic peptides when size is controlled — 62.4% pairwise accuracy within a three-atom window, where chance is 50% and a heavy-atom count reaches only 60.2% — at roughly a thousandth of the cost of rigorous free-energy simulation, which achieves 83.9% on the same pairs. At exactly matched size the point estimate is similar (60.1%) but the cohort does not contain enough same-size decisive pairs to separate it from chance at 95% confidence.

The methodological contribution is the comparison itself. Ligand size bias in scoring functions has been recognised for two decades,(Jacobsson & Karlén, 2006) and matched-pair benchmarks are an established response in small-molecule work.(Kalinowsky et al., 2018) Neither has been applied to macrocyclic peptides, where the size range within a series is far larger and where the usual correction — normalising by heavy-atom count or reporting ligand efficiency — is inappropriate because size is a mediator of the physics rather than a nuisance. Exact size matching sidesteps this: it requires no correction factor, makes no assumption about the functional form of the size dependence, and renders the control informative by construction.

What this licenses us to do. The protocol was established to decide which LptA designs to synthesise, and the validation above determines how far that decision can lean on it. Three constraints follow directly. Ranking is admissible within a branch, because that is what was tested; cross-branch ranking is not, because the branches occupy different score ranges. Size-matched selection is preferred, because that is the regime in which skill was demonstrated — which favours the thanatin branch and, within the de novo branch, a size-matched subset. And the selection must span the predicted range rather than take the top of it, because a set of predicted winners cannot test the ranking that chose them. Section 5 implements all three.

The practical reading for a design campaign is that this protocol is a triage filter, not a ranking to defend. A 60% edge is worth having when the alternative is arbitrary selection and the cost of being wrong is a thousand-dollar synthesis, particularly at seconds per compound. It is not worth defending against a rigorous calculation when the decision is expensive enough to justify one. The natural workflow is end-point scoring to reduce hundreds of candidates to tens, then alchemical calculation on the shortlist.

Three cautions generalise beyond this work.

The estimator matters. Pooling compounds drawn from different receptor structures can invert the sign of a result, as it does for KRAS (Table 4), so benchmark numbers computed that way should be treated sceptically — including when the pooling is hidden inside what is reported as a within-family metric.

Pose provenance matters. Where poses are built rather than crystallographic, scores can track construction artefact: on the 12CA5 panel the score correlated with the pose builder’s clash count at ρ = −0.891. Any end-point score should be reported alongside evidence about the geometry it was computed on.

Reference standards must themselves be validated. We could not settle whether force-field choice transfers between our datasets, because the only available reference on the design panel was a computational score that we measured at ρ = −0.149 against experiment (Section 3.6). Agreement with an unvalidated reference is not evidence.

3.11.1 Status and what follows

This paper establishes a method and reports what it supports. It does not report a validated prediction for LptA, and no such claim should be read into it. The sequence is deliberate: establish the method against measured data from other systems, determine its limits, apply it to the campaign panel under those limits, register the forward test, and only then commit synthetic resources. Synthesis and assay of the ten registered compounds is the immediate next step; the manuscript will be updated with those results, which Section 5 anticipates in both directions.

3.12 Limitations

  1. Five targets. Macro intervals rest on five values. Skill concentrates in PCSK9 and JAK2, and we could not identify why: polarity is the obvious candidate and it fails under both an interface and a binding-pocket definition (Section 3.4). With five targets we cannot distinguish a chemical explanation from chance.
  2. The strictest band is underpowered. At exactly equal heavy-atom count the cohort yields 337 decisive pairs in total, and the macro interval [0.472, 0.720] includes chance. Cyclin A/B is the extreme case, with 15 pairs and an interval spanning [0.053, 1.000]. The three-atom band is the better-powered analysis and the one we rely on.
  3. Only one target is individually significant. PCSK9 excludes chance at both bands; the other four do not. The macro result rests substantially on PCSK9, and a cohort without a polar-interface target might not reproduce it.
  4. Scores are not free energies (Section 3.5) and must not be quoted as predicted affinities.
  5. No measured affinities exist for the LptA designs. Section 4 is an application, not a validation, and Section 5 is a plan.
  6. Two selenium-containing non-canonical residues are approximations, GAFF2 having no selenium parameters.
  7. Single-structure scoring inherits whatever error the input pose carries. We verify pose quality explicitly (Section 4) but cannot certify that generated poses are correct.
  8. Censored measurements are excluded from pairwise analyses, which may bias the admitted set toward the measurable dynamic range.
  9. We evaluate the protocol as published, not an optimised variant. We did not re-tune the dielectric, solvation model or minimisation depth to maximise size-matched accuracy; doing so on five targets would overfit. The reported 60.1% is therefore a floor for this family of methods rather than the best achievable.

4. Conclusion

This work set out to establish, before committing synthetic resources, what an end-point scoring protocol can and cannot support for macrocyclic peptide design. Four conclusions follow.

First, size must be controlled explicitly, and normalisation is not the way to do it. For peptides, ligand size is a mediator of binding rather than a nuisance: experimental affinity tracks heavy-atom count at a mean within-target Spearman ρ of −0.43. Dividing a score by heavy atoms, or reporting ligand efficiency, therefore removes signal the physics is supposed to capture. Matching on size instead requires no correction factor and makes no assumption about the functional form of the dependence.

Second, the protocol has real but modest skill once size is controlled. Within a three-atom window it picks the tighter binder in 62.4% of decisive pairs (95% CI 55.5–68.9), against 50% for chance and 83.9% for published FEP+ on the same compounds. At exactly matched size the point estimate is comparable (60.1%) but the cohort does not contain enough same-size decisive pairs to separate it from chance. Its margin over a heavy-atom count at the chosen affinity threshold is only +0.022, widening to +0.07–0.20 for pairs separated by 1 kcal/mol or more.

Third, the skill is not uniform and the reasons are not identified. Only PCSK9 is individually above chance. Polarity is the obvious explanation and it fails under both an interface and a binding-pocket definition: JAK2 is fourth most polar of five yet second-highest at exact matching, and KRAS is second most polar and sits at chance. Replacing the molecular-mechanics energy function with a machine-learned force field does not help either, and leaves the method below a heavy-atom count (Section 3.6.1).

Fourth, benchmark performance on related targets is not evidence of transfer. On a sixth target held outside development, every method fell below chance and the size–affinity relationship reversed sign.

For the LptA campaign this licenses a bounded use: rank within branch, prefer size-matched comparisons, spend the alchemical budget on a shortlist rather than the full panel, and treat the output as triage rather than prediction. The ten compounds registered in Section 3.10 will test whether that holds prospectively; the power analysis stated there makes clear what such a test can and cannot establish at that scale.

6. Appendices

6.1 Appendix 1: Data and code availability

All code, computed scores, per-target statistics, bootstrap intervals and figures are available at https://github.com/Caroldorium/mmpbsa-macrocycle-benchmark under an MIT licence. scripts/size_matched_pairwise_accuracy.py reproduces Table 5 and the primary figure. so3lr_sf_evaluation/ holds the 241 SO3LR-SF scores, the pocket polar-SASA values, the splitting and scoring scripts and the code for Figure 5. Pairs are formed within a target and averaged across targets throughout; a pooled variant that compares compounds across targets gives materially different numbers and is retained only as a labelled diagnostic contrast.

Two third-party sources are reproduced for reproducibility and cited in place: measured affinities and FEP+ predictions from Awoonor-Williams et al.,(Awoonor-Williams et al., 2026) and the reference protocol and dataset tables from Zhao et al.(Zhao et al., 2025) All MM/PBSA scores, statistics, figures and code were computed in this work.

6.2 Appendix 2: Contributions and declarations

Author contributions. C.L. designed and executed the computational work, performed the analyses and wrote the manuscript. J.S.B. supervised the project and revised the manuscript. The prospective validation of Section 5 will be executed experimentally by the Brown laboratory.

Competing interests. The authors declare no competing financial interests.

Acknowledgements. Computations were performed on local GPU hardware and on the Digital Research Alliance of Canada national systems. We thank the authors of the two benchmark studies whose data made this evaluation possible.

6.3 Appendix 3: AI Appendix

Generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) was used in the preparation of this work. Its use is declared here in full.

The following tasks were carried out with AI assistance:

  1. Drafting and revision of the manuscript text across nine versions.
  2. Writing the analysis scripts that produce Tables 2–7 and Figures 2 and 4, and the pipeline schematic of Figure 1.
  3. Literature retrieval via PubMed, and verification of every reference against its database record.
  4. Auditing the draft against source data, which identified five errors in earlier versions (detailed below).

The output was checked and changed in the following ways:

  1. Every numerical claim was verified against the primary analysis files rather than against earlier drafts. This identified and corrected: a fabricated statistic (a perturbed-pose comparison that does not exist in the data); an incorrect design count (308 rather than 212); an incorrect range of spurious chain-break records; three unsupported sampling-convergence figures; and an incorrect bootstrap procedure that resampled non-independent pairs and so understated all confidence intervals by roughly half.
  2. The bootstrap correction changed a headline result: the exact-size-matched interval widened from [0.530, 0.693] to [0.472, 0.720] and no longer excludes chance. The affected claim was retracted and restated.
  3. All 19 references were verified against PubMed records; none were accepted as drafted.
  4. A complete record of every change across the nine versions, with the source file for verifying each, is retained in VERSION_REVIEW.md and VERSION_DIFFS.md in the deposited repository.

Scientific judgement, interpretation and the decision to publish remain the authors’. The underlying computational work — structure preparation, parameterisation, scoring and the benchmark calculations — was executed as described in Chapter 2 and is independent of the drafting assistance declared here.
